title: Ἡλίου μῆνις καὶ ναυάγιον
titleEn: The Sun’s Complaint and the Wreck — Odyssey 12.371–453
part: The Sun’s Complaint and the Wreck (12.371–453)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus finishes his cry to the gods: while he slept, his companions did a great wrong. Lampetie carries the news of the killed cattle to the Sun, who demands that Zeus punish the crew or he will go down to Hades and shine among the dead. Zeus tells him to keep shining and promises to split the ship with a thunderbolt; Odysseus says he heard this from Calypso, who had it from Hermes. On the shore Odysseus rebukes the men, but the cattle are dead, and the gods send portents: hides crawl and roasted meat lows. After six days of feasting the wind drops and they sail, but Zeus sets a dark cloud over the ship, the West Wind snaps the forestays, the falling mast kills the helmsman, and a thunderbolt wrecks the ship and drowns the men. Odysseus lashes keel and mast together and is driven back to Scylla and Charybdis, clings to a fig tree above the whirlpool until the keel and mast are thrown up again, and paddles away on them. After nine days he reaches Calypso’s island, and breaks off his tale because he told this part yesterday.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ ἠδ’ ἄλλοι μάκαρες θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες,
ἦ με μάλ’ εἰς ἄτην κοιμήσατε νηλέι ὕπνῳ.
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater ēd’ alloi makares theoi aien eontes,
ē me mal’ eis atēn koimēsate nēlei hypnōi.
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, and you other blessed gods who are forever,
truly indeed into ruin you lulled me with a pitiless sleep.
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, and you other blessed gods who are forever, you have indeed lulled me to my ruin with a pitiless sleep.
sentences.n: This is the cry that Odysseus began at 370 (‘I cried out loudly to the immortal gods’), so the quotation marks open here. The first line is the full address to Zeus and the other gods; θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες is ‘the gods who are forever’, with αἰέν the epic form of ἀεί and ἐόντες the participle of εἰμί. ἦ … μάλ’ is ‘truly, indeed’. In εἰς ἄτην the noun ἄτη is ‘ruin’, and it also means ‘delusion’. κοιμήσατε is the aorist of κοιμάω ‘put to sleep’, without augment, and νηλέι is the dative of νηλεής ‘pitiless’.
sentences.mark: Odysseus cries out to the gods

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἕταροι μέγα ἔργον ἐμητίσαντο μένοντες.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ hetaroi mega ergon emētisanto menontes.
sentences.l: and the companions a great deed devised, staying behind.”
sentences.i: while my companions, staying where they were, devised a great deed.”
sentences.n: ἕταροι is a short form of ἑταῖροι ‘companions’, and οἱ … ἕταροι is ‘they, the companions’: in Homer the article is a pronoun, with the noun added in apposition. μένοντες is the participle of μένω ‘stay, remain’: while he slept (372), the men stayed behind and acted. ἐμητίσαντο is the aorist middle of μητίομαι ‘devise, plan’, from μῆτις ‘cunning counsel’, and ‘a great deed’ is bitterly ironic. The closing quotation mark ends Odysseus’s cry.

sentences.t:
ὠκέα δ’ Ἠελίῳ Ὑπερίονι ἄγγελος ἦλθε
Λαμπετίη τανύπεπλος, ὅ οἱ βόας ἔκταμεν ἡμεῖς.
sentences.tr:
ōkea d’ Ēeliōi Hyperioni angelos ēlthe
Lampetiē tanypeplos, ho hoi boas ektamen hēmeis.
sentences.l:
swiftly to the Sun Hyperion a messenger came,
long-robed Lampetie, that his cattle we had killed.
sentences.i: And swiftly long-robed Lampetie came as a messenger to the Sun, Hyperion, to say that we had killed his cattle.
sentences.n: ὠκέα is formed from ὠκύς and is taken here as an adverb, ‘swiftly’ (it could also be the feminine ‘swift’, agreeing with Λαμπετίη). The messenger is Λαμπετίη, with τανύπεπλος ‘long-robed’ (τανύ- ‘long, stretched’ + πέπλος ‘robe’); Ἠελίῳ Ὑπερίονι is ‘the Sun Hyperion’, Hyperion being a name or epithet of the Sun himself. ὅ is here a conjunction, ‘that’ (the neuter of the relative), and οἱ is the dative ‘his’, ‘to him’. ἔκταμεν is a first-person plural aorist of κτείνω in an old short form (Attic ἐκτείναμεν); ἡμεῖς, ‘we’, is added for emphasis.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ ἀθανάτοισι μετηύδα χωόμενος κῆρ·
sentences.tr: autika d’ athanatoisi metēuda chōomenos kēr·
sentences.l: and at once among the immortals he spoke, angered in heart:
sentences.i: At once, angered in heart, he spoke among the immortals:
sentences.n: The subject is the Sun, named in 374. μετηύδα is from μεταυδάω ‘speak among’, here among the assembled gods, with ἀθανάτοισι ‘the immortals’ in the dative. χωόμενος κῆρ is ‘angered in heart’: χωόμενος is the participle of χώομαι ‘be angry’, and κῆρ ‘heart’ is an accusative of respect, naming the part affected. αὐτίκα is ‘at once’. The colon opens the Sun’s complaint.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ ἠδ’ ἄλλοι μάκαρες θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες,
τῖσαι δὴ ἑτάρους Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος,
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater ēd’ alloi makares theoi aien eontes,
tisai dē hetarous Laertiadeō Odysēos,
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, and you other blessed gods who are forever,
take vengeance now on the companions of the son of Laertes, Odysseus,
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, and you other blessed gods who are forever, take vengeance now on the companions of Odysseus, son of Laertes,
sentences.n: The first line is Odysseus’s own opening at 371, word for word, now in the Sun’s mouth. τῖσαι is the aorist middle imperative of τίνυμαι ‘exact a penalty from, punish’, hence ‘take vengeance on’; the active τίνω ‘pay’ returns as τίσουσι in 382, so that the demand and the condition echo each other. ἑτάρους is a short form of ἑταίρους. Λαερτιάδεω is a patronymic with the genitive -εω (Attic -ου), and Ὀδυσῆος has one σ where Ὀδυσσῆος has two: the poet uses whichever the verse needs.
sentences.mark: The Sun speaks to the gods

sentences.t:
οἵ μευ βοῦς ἔκτειναν ὑπέρβιον, ᾗσιν ἐγώ γε
χαίρεσκον μὲν ἰὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντα,
ἠδ’ ὁπότ’ ἂψ ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἀπ’ οὐρανόθεν προτραποίμην.
sentences.tr:
hoi meu bous ekteinan hyperbion, hēisin egō ge
chaireskon men iōn eis ouranon asteroenta,
ēd’ hopot’ aps epi gaian ap’ ouranothen protrapoimēn.
sentences.l:
who my cattle killed with exceeding violence, in which I
used to rejoice, going up into the starry sky,
and whenever back to the earth from the sky I turned.
sentences.i: who killed my cattle with exceeding violence, the cattle in which I used to take delight both when I climbed to the starry sky and whenever I turned back again from the sky to the earth.
sentences.n: μευ is the genitive μου ‘my’. ὑπέρβιον is an adverb, ‘with exceeding violence’ (ὑπέρ + βίη ‘force’). ᾗσιν is the dative plural feminine of ὅς, ‘in which’, referring back to βοῦς ‘cattle’, which is feminine here. χαίρεσκον is an imperfect in -σκ-, which marks a repeated action: ‘I used to rejoice’. The optative προτραποίμην after ὁπότε likewise means ‘whenever I turned’, a repeated event in past time. ἂψ is ‘back’, ἀστερόεντα ‘starry’, and οὐρανόθεν ‘from the sky’, with -θεν marking ‘from’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ μοι οὐ τίσουσι βοῶν ἐπιεικέ’ ἀμοιβήν,
δύσομαι εἰς Ἀίδαο καὶ ἐν νεκύεσσι φαείνω.
sentences.tr:
ei de moi ou tisousi boōn epieike’ amoibēn,
dysomai eis Aidao kai en nekyessi phaeinō.
sentences.l:
But if for me they will not pay a fitting recompense for the cattle,
I shall go down into Hades’ (house) and among the dead shine.”
sentences.i: But if they will not pay me a fitting recompense for the cattle, I shall go down to Hades and shine among the dead.”
sentences.n: δέ opens the condition that answers the demand of 378–381. τίσουσι is the future active of τίνω ‘pay’, the active counterpart of τῖσαι in 378. ἐπιεικέ’ is ἐπιεικέα ‘fitting’, and ἀμοιβήν is ‘exchange, recompense’, with βοῶν ‘for the cattle’. Ἀίδαο is the genitive of Ἀίδης ‘Hades’, with ‘house’ understood after εἰς. φαείνω is ‘I shine’, in form either a subjunctive or an indicative; in either case it continues the future δύσομαι. The threat is that the Sun will leave the sky for the dead. The closing quotation mark ends his speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to him:
sentences.n: A reply formula: ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ with προσέφη ‘addressed’, and τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, not the article. νεφεληγερέτα is Zeus’s epithet, ‘cloud-gatherer’ (νέφος ‘cloud’ + ἀγείρω ‘gather’); the ending -α is an old nominative form of nouns in -της. The colon introduces Zeus’s answer, which tells the Sun to go on shining and promises to wreck the ship.

sentences.t:
Ἠέλι’, ἦ τοι μὲν σὺ μετ’ ἀθανάτοισι φάεινε
καὶ θνητοῖσι βροτοῖσιν ἐπὶ ζείδωρον ἄρουραν·
sentences.tr:
Ēeli’, ē toi men sy met’ athanatoisi phaeine
kai thnētoisi brotoisin epi zeidōron arouran·
sentences.l:
“Sun, truly you among the immortals shine,
and for mortal men upon the grain-giving plough-land;
sentences.i: “Sun, you for your part go on shining among the immortals and for mortal men upon the grain-giving plough-land;
sentences.n: Ἠέλι’ is the vocative of Ἠέλιος ‘the Sun’, elided. ἦ τοι μέν is ‘truly, for your part’ and prepares the contrast of τῶν δέ in 387. φάεινε is the imperative of φαείνω, the verb the Sun used at 383. The second line is word for word 3.3, the line that describes the sun’s rising; ἄρουρα is ‘plough-land’, and ζείδωρος ‘grain-giving’ is the usual explanation of the adjective (‘life-giving’ is an ancient alternative).

sentences.t:
τῶν δέ κ’ ἐγὼ τάχα νῆα θοὴν ἀργῆτι κεραυνῷ
τυτθὰ βαλὼν κεάσαιμι μέσῳ ἐνὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ.
sentences.tr:
tōn de k’ egō tacha nēa thoēn argēti keraunōi
tyttha balōn keasaimi mesōi eni oinopi pontōi.
sentences.l:
but of them I soon the swift ship with the bright thunderbolt,
in small pieces striking it, would split in the middle of the wine-faced open-sea.”
sentences.i: But as for them, I would soon strike their swift ship with the bright thunderbolt and split it into small pieces in the middle of the sea that has the look of wine.”
sentences.n: τῶν is the genitive ‘their’, the crew’s, set against the Sun’s own work in the unit before. κεάσαιμι is the aorist optative of κεάζω ‘split’, with κε: ‘I would split’. τυτθά is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘in small pieces’, with βαλών ‘striking’. ἀργῆτι is the dative of ἀργής ‘bright’, and οἴνοπι the dative of οἴνοψ, the sea’s epithet, literally ‘wine-faced’. Zeus does exactly this at 415–417. The closing quotation mark ends his speech.

sentences.t: ταῦτα δ’ ἐγὼν ἤκουσα Καλυψοῦς ἠυκόμοιο·
sentences.tr: tauta d’ egōn ēkousa Kalypsous ēykomoio·
sentences.l: And these things I heard from Calypso, fine-haired;
sentences.i: These things I heard from fine-haired Calypso;
sentences.n: Odysseus could not have been present in heaven, and he now says where he learned what was said there. ἐγών is a form of ἐγώ ‘I’; ἤκουσα takes the genitive of the person heard from, Καλυψοῦς. ἠυκόμοιο is the genitive of ἠύκομος ‘fine-haired’, in -οιο (Attic -ου); it is a different adjective from the ἐυπλόκαμος ‘fine-plaited’ used of Calypso at 449.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἔφη Ἑρμείαο διακτόρου αὐτὴ ἀκοῦσαι.
sentences.tr: hē d’ ephē Hermeiao diaktorou autē akousai.
sentences.l: and she said that from Hermes the guide herself she had heard.
sentences.i: and she said she had heard it herself from Hermes, the guide.
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, Calypso. ἔφη ‘she said’ takes an infinitive, ἀκοῦσαι, the aorist of ἀκούω ‘hear’, so the construction is ‘she said that she heard’; αὐτή ‘herself’ is nominative because the subject is the same. Ἑρμείαο is a genitive in -αο of the source, ‘from Hermes’. διάκτορος is Hermes’s standing epithet; its meaning is not known, and ‘guide’ is only the traditional guess.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλυθον ἠδὲ θάλασσαν,
νείκεον ἄλλοθεν ἄλλον ἐπισταδόν, οὐδέ τι μῆχος
εὑρέμεναι δυνάμεσθα, βόες δ’ ἀποτέθνασαν ἤδη.
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ epi nēa katēlython ēde thalassan,
neikeon allothen allon epistadon, oude ti mēchos
heuremenai dynamestha, boes d’ apotethnasan ēdē.
sentences.l:
But when then I had come down to the ship and the sea,
I reviled them, from different places one after another, standing by each, and not any remedy
were we able to find, for the cattle had died already.
sentences.i: And when I had come down to the ship and the sea, I reviled them one after another, standing by each man, but we could find no remedy, for the cattle were already dead.
sentences.n: The first line is used elsewhere in the poem with ‘they’ as its subject; here κατήλυθον is first person, ‘I had come down’, since it is Odysseus who goes down to the men; νείκεον ‘I reviled’ (imperfect of νεικέω, a form that could also be third plural) agrees, and δυνάμεσθα ‘we were able’ then widens the subject to the whole company. ἄλλοθεν ἄλλον is ‘one man from one place, another from another’, that is, each in turn; ἐπισταδόν is ‘standing close by’. μῆχος is ‘means, remedy’, and εὑρέμεναι is the infinitive ‘to find’ in -μεναι. ἀποτέθνασαν is a past perfect without augment, ‘had died’.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα θεοὶ τέραα προύφαινον·
sentences.tr: toisin d’ autik’ epeita theoi teraa prouphainon·
sentences.l: And to them at once then the gods were showing portents:
sentences.i: And at once the gods began to show them portents:
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is the pronoun, ‘to them’, in the dative -οισιν. τέραα is the plural of τέρας ‘portent, sign’ (Attic τέρατα). προύφαινον is the imperfect of προφαίνω ‘show forth’, the augment having run together with προ-, and the tense suggests a series of signs, not one. The colon announces the portents described in the next two lines.

sentences.t:
εἷρπον μὲν ῥινοί, κρέα δ’ ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσι μεμύκει,
ὀπταλέα τε καὶ ὠμά, βοῶν δ’ ὣς γίγνετο φωνή.
sentences.tr:
heirpon men rhinoi, krea d’ amph’ obeloisi memykei,
optalea te kai ōma, boōn d’ hōs gigneto phōnē.
sentences.l:
crawled the hides, and the flesh around the spits lowed,
roasted and raw alike, and of cattle so came the voice.
sentences.i: The hides crawled, and the meat lowed upon the spits, roasted and raw alike, and the sound that came was the voice of cattle.
sentences.n: εἷρπον is the imperfect of ἕρπω ‘creep, crawl’, and ῥινοί are the ‘hides’, the flayed skins. κρέα is a neuter plural, ‘pieces of meat’, which takes a singular verb: μεμύκει is the past perfect of μυκάομαι ‘low, bellow’, used like an imperfect, ‘was lowing’. ὀβελοῖσι is a dative plural ‘spits’. ὀπταλέα ‘roasted’ (from ὀπτάω) and ὠμά ‘raw’ agree with κρέα. ὣς with the circumflex is the adverb ‘so, in that way’: the sound was the voice of cattle.

sentences.t:
ἑξῆμαρ μὲν ἔπειτα ἐμοὶ ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι
δαίνυντ’ Ἠελίοιο βοῶν ἐλάσαντες ἀρίστας·
sentences.tr:
hexēmar men epeita emoi eriēres hetairoi
dainynt’ Ēelioio boōn elasantes aristas·
sentences.l:
For six days then my trusty companions
feasted, of the Sun’s cattle having driven off the best;
sentences.i: For six days then my trusty companions feasted, having driven off the best of the Sun’s cattle;
sentences.n: ἑξῆμαρ is the adverb ‘for six days’, and μέν looks forward to ἀλλ’ ὅτε in 399. ἐμοί is a dative ‘my’, literally ‘to me’. ἐρίηρες is ‘trusty’; the sense of ἐρίηρος is not fully known. δαίνυντ’ is the elided imperfect middle of δαίνυμι ‘feast’. Ἠελίοιο βοῶν ἐλάσαντες ἀρίστας is the phrase Eurylochus used at 343 and the men acted on at 353; ἐλάσαντες is the aorist participle of ἐλαύνω, ‘driving off’ cattle.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ἕβδομον ἦμαρ ἐπὶ Ζεὺς θῆκε Κρονίων,
καὶ τότ’ ἔπειτ’ ἄνεμος μὲν ἐπαύσατο λαίλαπι θύων,
ἡμεῖς δ’ αἶψ’ ἀναβάντες ἐνήκαμεν εὐρέι πόντῳ,
ἱστὸν στησάμενοι ἀνά θ’ ἱστία λεύκ’ ἐρύσαντες.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē hebdomon ēmar epi Zeus thēke Kroniōn,
kai tot’ epeit’ anemos men epausato lailapi thyōn,
hēmeis d’ aips’ anabantes enēkamen eurei pontōi,
histon stēsamenoi ana th’ histia leuk’ erysantes.
sentences.l:
But when indeed the seventh day Zeus set on, the son of Cronus,
then thereupon the wind ceased raging with a squall,
and we quickly going up launched on the broad open-sea,
the mast having set up and the white sails having hoisted.
sentences.i: But when Zeus, the son of Cronus, added the seventh day, then the wind stopped raging in its squalls, and we went aboard quickly and launched out on the broad sea, setting up the mast and hoisting the white sails.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … θῆκε is tmesis, ‘added’. Κρονίων is a patronymic, ‘son of Cronus’, here a name for Zeus. ἐπαύσατο with a participle means ‘ceased doing’: the wind ceased λαίλαπι θύων, ‘raging with a squall’. ἐνήκαμεν is from ἐνίημι, ‘let in, launch’, with the ship understood. ἱστόν is the ship’s mast (the same word is the weaver’s loom); στησάμενοι ‘having set up’, and ἀνά … ἐρύσαντες is tmesis, ‘having hoisted’; ἱστία are the sails, λεύκ’ ‘white’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὴν νῆσον ἐλείπομεν, οὐδέ τις ἄλλη
φαίνετο γαιάων, ἀλλ’ οὐρανὸς ἠδὲ θάλασσα,
δὴ τότε κυανέην νεφέλην ἔστησε Κρονίων
νηὸς ὕπερ γλαφυρῆς, ἤχλυσε δὲ πόντος ὑπ’ αὐτῆς.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē tēn nēson eleipomen, oude tis allē
phaineto gaiaōn, all’ ouranos ēde thalassa,
dē tote kyaneēn nephelēn estēse Kroniōn
nēos hyper glaphyrēs, ēchlyse de pontos hyp’ autēs.
sentences.l:
But when indeed we were leaving the island, and no other
land appeared, but sky and sea,
then indeed a dark cloud the son of Cronus set
over the hollow ship, and the open-sea grew dim beneath it.
sentences.i: But when we left the island behind, and no other land came into sight, only sky and sea, then the son of Cronus set a dark cloud above the hollow ship, and the sea grew dim beneath it.
sentences.n: τὴν νῆσον is ‘the island’, the island of the Sun’s cattle, to which the article points back. ἐλείπομεν is the imperfect ‘we were leaving’. οὐδέ τις ἄλλη … γαιάων is ‘no other of lands’, a partitive genitive. κυανέην ‘dark’ is the colour-word seen in κυανοχαίτης ‘dark-haired’. ἔστησε is ‘set, stood’, and the cloud is Zeus’s doing, the first step in the storm. ἤχλυσε is from ἀχλύω ‘grow misty, dim’, from ἀχλύς ‘haze’; ὑπ’ αὐτῆς is ‘beneath it’, the cloud.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἔθει οὐ μάλα πολλὸν ἐπὶ χρόνον·
sentences.tr: hē d’ ethei ou mala pollon epi chronon·
sentences.l: And she ran for not very long a time;
sentences.i: She ran on for no very long time;
sentences.n: ἡ is a pronoun, ‘she’, the ship (νηῦς is feminine, named at 406). ἔθει is the imperfect of θέω ‘run’, used of a ship under way. πολλόν is the epic form of πολύν, with the doubled λ, ‘long’ with χρόνον. The pause (the Greek ano teleia) prepares the explanation, αἶψα γὰρ, ‘for quickly’.

sentences.t:
αἶψα γὰρ ἦλθε
κεκληγὼς Ζέφυρος μεγάλῃ σὺν λαίλαπι θύων,
ἱστοῦ δὲ προτόνους ἔρρηξ’ ἀνέμοιο θύελλα
ἀμφοτέρους·
sentences.tr:
aipsa gar ēlthe
keklēgōs Zephyros megalēi syn lailapi thyōn,
histou de protonous errēx’ anemoio thyella
amphoterous·
sentences.l:
for quickly came
screaming the West Wind, with a great squall raging,
and of the mast the forestays snapped a storm-blast of wind,
both;
sentences.i: for quickly the West Wind came, screaming and raging with a great squall, and a storm-blast of wind snapped both forestays of the mast;
sentences.n: κεκληγώς is the perfect participle of κλάζω ‘scream, shriek’, with a present sense. Ζέφυρος is ‘the West Wind’, and μεγάλῃ σὺν λαίλαπι θύων is ‘raging with a great squall’, the same participle as at 400. προτόνους are the forestays, the ropes that held the mast forward to the bow; ἔρρηξ’ is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break, snap’; ἀνέμοιο θύελλα is ‘a storm-blast of wind’. ἀμφοτέρους ‘both’ opens line 410, after the verb has already been given.

sentences.t:
ἱστὸς δ’ ὀπίσω πέσεν, ὅπλα τε πάντα
εἰς ἄντλον κατέχυνθ’.
sentences.tr:
histos d’ opisō pesen, hopla te panta
eis antlon katechynth’.
sentences.l:
and the mast backward fell, and all the gear
into the bilge was poured down.
sentences.i: and the mast fell backward, and all the gear was poured down into the bilge.
sentences.n: ἱστός is the mast again. ὀπίσω is ‘backward’, toward the stern: with the forestays gone the mast falls aft, which prepares the next unit. ὅπλα is the plural of ὅπλον ‘gear’, here the ship’s tackle. ἄντλος is the bilge, the foul water and hollow at the bottom of the hull. κατέχυνθ’ is the elided aorist passive of καταχέω ‘pour down’, plural in sense.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρα πρυμνῇ ἐνὶ νηὶ
πλῆξε κυβερνήτεω κεφαλήν, σὺν δ’ ὀστέ’ ἄραξε
πάντ’ ἄμυδις κεφαλῆς·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ara prymnēi eni nēi
plēxe kybernēteō kephalēn, syn d’ oste’ araxe
pant’ amydis kephalēs·
sentences.i: and it struck the helmsman on the head in the stern of the ship and crushed all the bones of his head together;
sentences.n: ὁ is a pronoun, ‘it’, the falling mast. πρυμνῇ ἐνὶ νηί is ‘in the stern of the ship’, πρυμνός being ‘hindmost’. κυβερνήτεω is the genitive of κυβερνήτης ‘helmsman’, in -εω. σὺν … ἄραξε is tmesis, ‘crushed together’, from ἀράσσω ‘smash’, and πάντ’ ἄμυδις adds ‘all together’, so the picture is of complete crushing. κεφαλῆς ‘of the head’ is a genitive of the whole with ὀστέ’ ‘the bones’.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀρνευτῆρι ἐοικὼς
κάππεσ’ ἀπ’ ἰκριόφιν, λίπε δ’ ὀστέα θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ arneutēri eoikōs
kappes’ ap’ ikriophin, lipe d’ ostea thymos agēnōr.
sentences.l:
and he, like a diver,
fell down from the decking, and left his bones the manly spirit.
sentences.i: and he, like a diver, tumbled from the decking, and his proud spirit left his bones.
sentences.n: Here ὁ is the helmsman. ἀρνευτῆρι is the dative of ἀρνευτήρ, one who plunges headfirst, a ‘diver’, with ἐοικώς ‘like’. κάππεσ’ is κατέπεσε, with the τ of κατ- assimilated to the following π: ‘fell down’. ἰκριόφιν is ‘from the decking’, the suffix -φιν doing the work of a case ending. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is a set phrase: θυμός is the life-spirit that leaves the body at death, and ἀγήνωρ means ‘manly, proud’.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς δ’ ἄμυδις βρόντησε καὶ ἔμβαλε νηὶ κεραυνόν·
sentences.tr: Zeus d’ amydis brontēse kai embale nēi keraunon·
sentences.l: And Zeus together thundered and cast into the ship a thunderbolt;
sentences.i: Then Zeus thundered and, at the same moment, hurled a thunderbolt into the ship;
sentences.n: Zeus now does what he promised at 387–388. ἄμυδις is ‘together, at the same time’: the thunder and the bolt are one event. βρόντησε is the aorist of βροντάω ‘thunder’. ἔμβαλε is from ἐμβάλλω ‘throw in’, with the dative νηί ‘into the ship’; the augment is absent, as often in Homer. κεραυνός is the thunderbolt, the weapon itself.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἐλελίχθη πᾶσα Διὸς πληγεῖσα κεραυνῷ,
ἐν δὲ θεείου πλῆτο, πέσον δ’ ἐκ νηὸς ἑταῖροι.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ elelichthē pasa Dios plēgeisa keraunōi,
en de theeiou plēto, peson d’ ek nēos hetairoi.
sentences.l:
and she shook all over, struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus,
and with sulphur was filled, and fell from the ship the companions.
sentences.i: She shook from end to end, struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus, and was filled with sulphur, and the companions fell out of the ship.
sentences.n: ἡ is the ship. ἐλελίχθη is the aorist passive of ἐλελίζω ‘shake, make quiver’; πᾶσα is ‘all over’. Διὸς … κεραυνῷ is ‘by the thunderbolt of Zeus’, a dative of means. ἐν … πλῆτο is tmesis of ἐμπίμπλημι ‘fill’, with the genitive θεείου, ‘sulphur’, the smell that follows a lightning stroke. πέσον is an aorist without augment, ‘fell’; ἐκ νηός ‘out of the ship’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ κορώνῃσιν ἴκελοι περὶ νῆα μέλαιναν
κύμασιν ἐμφορέοντο, θεὸς δ’ ἀποαίνυτο νόστον.
sentences.tr:
hoi de korōnēisin ikeloi peri nēa melainan
kymasin emphoreonto, theos d’ apoainyto noston.
sentences.l:
and they, like crows, around the black ship
on the waves were carried about, and the god took away their homecoming.
sentences.i: And they, like crows, were carried about the black ship on the waves, and the god took away their homecoming.
sentences.n: κορώνῃσιν is the dative plural of κορώνη, ‘crow’, a word also used of sea-birds; which bird is meant is not certain. ἴκελοι ‘like’ takes the dative. ἐμφορέοντο is the imperfect passive of ἐμφορέω ‘carry about in’, κύμασιν ‘on the waves’. θεός has no article in Greek; the god is Zeus, named in 415. ἀποαίνυτο is an unaugmented past tense of ἀπαίνυμαι ‘take away’. The loss of the homecoming is the end announced in the proem (1.9, ‘took from them the day of their homecoming’).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ διὰ νηὸς ἐφοίτων, ὄφρ’ ἀπὸ τοίχους
λῦσε κλύδων τρόπιος, τὴν δὲ ψιλὴν φέρε κῦμα,
ἐκ δέ οἱ ἱστὸν ἄραξε ποτὶ τρόπιν.
sentences.tr:
autar egō dia nēos ephoitōn, ophr’ apo toichous
lyse klydōn tropios, tēn de psilēn phere kyma,
ek de hoi histon araxe poti tropin.
sentences.l:
But I through the ship kept going to and fro, until away the sides
the surge loosed from the keel, and it, stripped bare, the wave carried,
and out of it the mast it dashed against the keel.
sentences.i: But I kept moving to and fro through the ship until the surge loosened her sides from the keel; the wave carried the bare keel along and, tearing the mast out of the ship, dashed it against the keel.
sentences.n: ἐφοίτων is the imperfect of φοιτάω ‘go to and fro’. ὄφρα ‘until’ takes the aorist. ἀπὸ … λῦσε is tmesis, ‘loosed away’; τοίχους are literally ‘walls’, here the sides of the hull, and τρόπιος, genitive of τρόπις ‘keel’, gives what they were loosed from. ψιλήν ‘bare’ is the keel stripped of its planking; φέρε is unaugmented. ἐκ … ἄραξε is tmesis, ‘dashed out’; οἱ is a dative ‘to it’, the ship, which with ἐκ gives ‘out of it’, and ποτί is πρός ‘against’. The subject of both verbs is κῦμα ‘the wave’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ
ἐπίτονος βέβλητο, βοὸς ῥινοῖο τετευχώς·
sentences.tr:
autar ep’ autōi
epitonos beblēto, boos rhinoio teteuchōs·
sentences.l:
but upon it
a backstay had been thrown, made of ox-hide;
sentences.i: and on it lay a backstay, made of oxhide;
sentences.n: ἐπ’ αὐτῷ is ‘upon it’, the mast (masculine, as τρόπιν is not). ἐπίτονος is a rope belonging to the mast; ‘backstay’ is the usual guess, and its exact fitting is not known. βέβλητο is the past perfect passive of βάλλω ‘throw’, ‘had been thrown, lay’. βοὸς ῥινοῖο is ‘of ox-hide’, a genitive in -οιο, and τετευχώς, the perfect participle of τεύχω ‘make’, has a passive sense, ‘made of’. Line 423 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of ἐπίτονος, short by nature, has to be read long to make the first foot.

sentences.t:
τῷ ῥ’ ἄμφω συνέεργον, ὁμοῦ τρόπιν ἠδὲ καὶ ἱστόν,
ἑζόμενος δ’ ἐπὶ τοῖς φερόμην ὀλοοῖς ἀνέμοισιν.
sentences.tr:
tōi rh’ amphō syneergon, homou tropin ēde kai histon,
hezomenos d’ epi tois pheromēn oloois anemoisin.
sentences.l:
with it then I bound both together, jointly the keel and the mast as well,
and sitting upon them I was carried by deadly winds.
sentences.i: With it I lashed the two together, keel and mast alike, and sat on them and was carried by deadly winds.
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘with it’, the oxhide stay, a dative of means. ῥ’ is ῥα, a small particle that marks what follows from what went before. ἄμφω is ‘both’, and συνέεργον, from συνέργω, is ‘I bound together’, imperfect first person. ὁμοῦ is ‘together’. ἑζόμενος is the participle of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’. ὀλοοῖς is the dative plural of ὀλοός ‘deadly’, agreeing with the dative of means ἀνέμοισιν ‘by the winds’, in -οισιν.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι Ζέφυρος μὲν ἐπαύσατο λαίλαπι θύων,
ἦλθε δ’ ἐπὶ Νότος ὦκα, φέρων ἐμῷ ἄλγεα θυμῷ,
ὄφρ’ ἔτι τὴν ὀλοὴν ἀναμετρήσαιμι Χάρυβδιν.
sentences.tr:
enth’ ē toi Zephyros men epausato lailapi thyōn,
ēlthe d’ epi Notos ōka, pherōn emōi algea thymōi,
ophr’ eti tēn oloēn anametrēsaimi Charybdin.
sentences.l:
Then indeed the West Wind ceased raging with a squall,
and there came on the South Wind quickly, bringing to my heart pains,
so that still the deadly Charybdis I should measure back again.
sentences.i: Then the West Wind stopped raging in its squalls, and the South Wind came on quickly, bringing pains to my heart, so that I should once more have to retrace my way over deadly Charybdis.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι is ‘then indeed’. ἐπαύσατο … θύων is the same ‘ceased raging’ as at 400. ἐπὶ … ἦλθε is tmesis, ‘came on’; Νότος is ‘the South Wind’, ὦκα ‘quickly’. ἐμῷ … θυμῷ ‘to my heart’ is a dative of the person affected. ὄφρα with the optative gives the result aimed at, ‘so that I should’; ἀναμετρήσαιμι is from ἀναμετρέω ‘measure back, retrace’, and ἔτι is ‘still, further’. The South Wind drives him back to the monster he had passed.

sentences.t:
παννύχιος φερόμην, ἅμα δ’ ἠελίῳ ἀνιόντι
ἦλθον ἐπὶ Σκύλλης σκόπελον δεινήν τε Χάρυβδιν.
sentences.tr:
pannychios pheromēn, hama d’ ēeliōi anionti
ēlthon epi Skyllēs skopelon deinēn te Charybdin.
sentences.l:
All night long I was carried, and with the rising sun
I came to the crag of Scylla and to dread Charybdis.
sentences.i: All night I was carried along, and at sunrise I came to the crag of Scylla and to dread Charybdis.
sentences.n: παννύχιος is an adjective used as an adverb, ‘all night long’. ἅμα with the dative ἠελίῳ ἀνιόντι is ‘together with the rising sun’; ἀνιόντι is the participle of ἄνειμι ‘go up’. σκόπελος is a ‘crag’, a rocky outlook, and Σκύλλης σκόπελον is ‘Scylla’s crag’. δεινήν ‘dread’ is the epithet Charybdis has here, not the ὀλοήν ‘deadly’ of 428.

sentences.t: ἡ μὲν ἀνερροίβδησε θαλάσσης ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ·
sentences.tr: hē men anerroibdēse thalassēs halmyron hydōr·
sentences.l: she on the one hand sucked down the sea’s salt water;
sentences.i: Charybdis, for her part, sucked down the salt water of the sea;
sentences.n: ἡ is ‘she’, Charybdis. μέν sets her act against αὐτὰρ ἐγώ ‘but I’ in the next line. ἀνερροίβδησε is the aorist of ἀναρροιβδέω ‘suck down’, built on ῥοῖβδος, the rushing noise of water. θαλάσσης is a genitive, ‘of the sea’, with ὕδωρ; ἁλμυρόν is ‘salt’, from ἅλς ‘salt, sea’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ ποτὶ μακρὸν ἐρινεὸν ὑψόσ’ ἀερθείς,
τῷ προσφὺς ἐχόμην ὡς νυκτερίς.
sentences.tr:
autar egō poti makron erineon hypsos’ aertheis,
tōi prosphys echomēn hōs nykteris.
sentences.l:
but I, toward the tall wild fig tree, lifted up on high,
clinging to it, held on like a bat.
sentences.i: But I was lifted up to the tall wild fig tree and, clinging to it, held on like a bat.
sentences.n: ἐρινεός is the ‘wild fig tree’, and μακρόν ‘long’ is ‘tall’ of a tree. ὑψόσ’ is ‘up on high’, and ἀερθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’: the surge or draught lifts him; the Greek does not say which. προσφύς is the aorist participle ‘having grown fast to’, with ἐχόμην ‘I held on’ (imperfect middle of ἔχω). νυκτερίς is a ‘bat’, literally the night creature; ὡς without an accent is ‘like’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ πῃ εἶχον
οὔτε στηρίξαι ποσὶν ἔμπεδον οὔτ’ ἐπιβῆναι·
sentences.tr:
oude pēi eichon
oute stērixai posin empedon out’ epibēnai·
sentences.l:
and in no way could I
either brace my feet firmly or step upon it;
sentences.i: and I could find no way either to brace my feet firmly or to climb onto it;
sentences.n: εἶχον with an infinitive means ‘was able’, as ἔχω ‘have’ can in Homer. πῃ is an indefinite ‘in any way’, so οὐδέ πῃ is ‘nor in any way’. στηρίξαι is the aorist infinitive of στηρίζω ‘prop, brace’, and ἔμπεδον ‘firmly’ is an adverb. ἐπιβῆναι is the aorist infinitive of ἐπιβαίνω ‘step onto’; the tree is understood. The pair οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’; the reason follows in the next line.

sentences.t:
ῥίζαι γὰρ ἑκὰς εἶχον, ἀπήωροι δ’ ἔσαν ὄζοι,
μακροί τε μεγάλοι τε, κατεσκίαον δὲ Χάρυβδιν.
sentences.tr:
rhizai gar hekas eichon, apēōroi d’ esan ozoi,
makroi te megaloi te, kateskiaon de Charybdin.
sentences.l:
for the roots were far off, and hanging aloft were the branches,
long and great, and they overshadowed Charybdis.
sentences.i: For its roots lay far away, and its branches hung aloft, long and great, and they overshadowed Charybdis.
sentences.n: ῥίζαι is ‘roots’, and ἑκὰς εἶχον is literally ‘held far off’, that is, lay far below out of reach. ἀπήωροι is ‘hanging aloft’, from ἀπό and ἀείρω; ὄζοι are ‘branches’. ἔσαν is the epic ἦσαν ‘were’. μακροί ‘long’ and μεγάλοι ‘great’ are plural nominatives agreeing with ὄζοι. κατεσκίαον is the imperfect of κατασκιάω, the epic form of κατασκιάζω ‘overshadow’: the branches stretch out above the whirlpool.

sentences.t:
νωλεμέως δ’ ἐχόμην, ὄφρ’ ἐξεμέσειεν ὀπίσσω
ἱστὸν καὶ τρόπιν αὖτις·
sentences.tr:
nōlemeōs d’ echomēn, ophr’ exemeseien opissō
histon kai tropin autis·
sentences.l:
And unceasingly I held on, until she should vomit out backward
the mast and the keel, again;
sentences.i: I held on without letting go, until she should vomit up the mast and the keel again;
sentences.n: νωλεμέως is ‘unceasingly, without slackening’. ὄφρα with the optative ἐξεμέσειεν means ‘until she should vomit out’, expressing what he waits and hopes for, from ἐξεμέω ‘vomit forth’; the subject is Charybdis. ὀπίσσω is ‘back’ and αὖτις ‘again’: the whirlpool must return what it swallowed. ἱστὸν καὶ τρόπιν ‘the mast and the keel’ are the wreckage he had lashed together at 424.

sentences.t:
ἐελδομένῳ δέ μοι ἦλθον
ὄψ’·
sentences.tr:
eeldomenōi de moi ēlthon
ops’·
sentences.l:
and to me, longing, they came
late;
sentences.i: and, as I longed for them, they came late;
sentences.n: ἐελδομένῳ is the participle of ἐέλδομαι ‘long for’, in the dative to agree with μοι ‘to me’. ἦλθον is plural, ‘they came’, the mast and the keel. ὄψ’ is the elided ὀψέ ‘late’, and the pause after it prepares the long description of the hour in the next unit. The dative ἐελδομένῳ … μοι names the person for whom they were late.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἐπὶ δόρπον ἀνὴρ ἀγορῆθεν ἀνέστη
κρίνων νείκεα πολλὰ δικαζομένων αἰζηῶν,
τῆμος δὴ τά γε δοῦρα Χαρύβδιος ἐξεφαάνθη.
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ epi dorpon anēr agorēthen anestē
krinōn neikea polla dikazomenōn aizēōn,
tēmos dē ta ge doura Charybdios exephaanthē.
sentences.l:
at the time when for supper a man from the assembly rises,
judging the many quarrels of vigorous men going to law,
at that time indeed those timbers from Charybdis appeared.
sentences.i: It was the hour when a man rises from the assembly for his supper, after judging the many quarrels of the vigorous men who go to law; then at last those timbers appeared out of Charybdis.
sentences.n: ἦμος … τῆμος is ‘when … then’, an epic pair. ἀγορῆθεν is ‘from the assembly’, with -θεν. ἀνέστη is an aorist used of what a man regularly does, ‘rises’. κρίνων is ‘judging, deciding’; δικαζομένων is the middle participle of δικάζω ‘go to law, plead’, and αἰζηῶν ‘vigorous men’. The time meant is the hour of the evening meal. τά γε δοῦρα is ‘those timbers’, δοῦρα being the plural of δόρυ ‘wood, timber’ (the same word means ‘spear’). Χαρύβδιος is the genitive of Χάρυβδις, with ἐξεφαάνθη ‘appeared out’.

sentences.t:
ἧκα δ’ ἐγὼ καθύπερθε πόδας καὶ χεῖρε φέρεσθαι,
μέσσῳ δ’ ἐνδούπησα παρὲξ περιμήκεα δοῦρα,
ἑζόμενος δ’ ἐπὶ τοῖσι διήρεσα χερσὶν ἐμῇσι.
sentences.tr:
hēka d’ egō kathyperthe podas kai cheire pheresthai,
messōi d’ endoupēsa parex perimēkea doura,
hezomenos d’ epi toisi diēresa chersin emēisi.
sentences.l:
And I let go from above my feet and hands to be carried down,
and into the middle I fell with a thud, beside the very long timbers,
and sitting upon them I rowed through with my own hands.
sentences.i: I let my feet and hands go and dropped from above, and fell with a thud into the middle, beside the very long timbers; then, sitting on them, I rowed my way with my own hands.
sentences.n: ἧκα is the aorist of ἵημι ‘let go’, with the infinitive φέρεσθαι, ‘to be carried’, so he lets his hands and feet drop from the branch; χεῖρε is a dual, ‘both hands’. καθύπερθε is ‘from above’. ἐνδούπησα is from ἐνδουπέω ‘fall with a thud’ (cf. δοῦπος ‘thud’). παρέξ with the accusative is ‘out beside’, and περιμήκεα ‘very long’. διήρεσα is from διερέσσω ‘row through’, the hands serving as oars. ἐμῇσι is the dative plural ‘my own’.

sentences.t:
Σκύλλην δ’ οὐκέτ’ ἔασε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε
εἰσιδέειν·
sentences.tr:
Skyllēn d’ ouket’ ease patēr andrōn te theōn te
eisideein·
sentences.l:
But Scylla no longer allowed the father of men and of gods
to see;
sentences.i: But the father of men and of gods no longer let me look upon Scylla;
sentences.n: ἔασε is the aorist of ἐάω ‘allow’; its object, ‘me’, is understood. εἰσιδέειν is the aorist infinitive of εἰσοράω ‘look upon’, in the epic ending -έειν (Attic -εῖν). The father of men and of gods is Zeus, and the phrase is a formula. The pause after εἰσιδέειν prepares the reason, which follows.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ κεν ὑπέκφυγον αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr: ou gar ken hypekphygon aipyn olethron.
sentences.l: for I would not have escaped steep destruction.
sentences.i: for I would not have escaped steep destruction.
sentences.n: κεν with an aorist indicative gives a past potential, ‘I would not have escaped’; ὑπέκφυγον is the aorist of ὑπεκφεύγω ‘escape from under’, with no augment. αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον ‘steep destruction’ is a phrase of the poem, found at 1.11 and 1.37. The reason is given in the clause itself: to see Scylla would have meant meeting her.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δ’ ἐννῆμαρ φερόμην, δεκάτῃ δέ με νυκτὶ
νῆσον ἐς Ὠγυγίην πέλασαν θεοί, ἔνθα Καλυψὼ
ναίει ἐυπλόκαμος, δεινὴ θεὸς αὐδήεσσα,
ἥ μ’ ἐφίλει τ’ ἐκόμει τε.
sentences.tr:
enthen d’ ennēmar pheromēn, dekatēi de me nykti
nēson es Ōgygiēn pelasan theoi, entha Kalypsō
naiei eyplokamos, deinē theos audēessa,
hē m’ ephilei t’ ekomei te.
sentences.l:
From there for nine days I was carried, and on the tenth night me
to the Ogygian island brought-near the gods, where Calypso
dwells, fine-plaited, a dread goddess endowed with speech,
who me loved and tended.
sentences.i: From there for nine days I was carried, and on the tenth night the gods brought me near to the island of Ogygia, where Calypso dwells, fine-plaited, a dread goddess who speaks with a human voice, who loved me and tended me.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν is ‘from there’, and ἐννῆμαρ ‘for nine days’. δεκάτῃ … νυκτί is a dative of time, ‘on the tenth night’. πέλασαν is an aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near’, without augment; Ὠγυγίην is ‘Ogygian’, of Ogygia. ναίει ‘dwells’; ἐυπλόκαμος ‘fine-plaited’, and δεινὴ θεὸς αὐδήεσσα is ‘a dread goddess endowed with speech’, the force of αὐδήεσσα being debated (the ancient explanation is ‘with a human voice’). ἥ is the relative ‘who’; ἐκόμει is from κομέω ‘tend, care for’.

sentences.t: τί τοι τάδε μυθολογεύω;
sentences.tr: ti toi tade mythologeuō;
sentences.l: Why to you these things do I tell over?
sentences.i: Why do I tell all this over to you?
sentences.n: τοι is the enclitic dative ‘to you’ (σοι). τάδε is ‘these things’. μυθολογεύω is formed on μῦθος ‘tale’ and λέγω, and means ‘tell as a tale, relate’; it comes again in the last line. The question is rhetorical: Odysseus turns to the host he is addressing and asks why he should tell this over, since, as the next lines say, he has told it already.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ τοι χθιζὸς ἐμυθεόμην ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
σοί τε καὶ ἰφθίμῃ ἀλόχῳ·
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar toi chthizos emytheomēn eni oikōi
soi te kai iphthimēi alochōi·
sentences.l:
For already yesterday I told it in the house
to you and to your mighty wife;
sentences.i: For I told it yesterday, in the house, to you and to your mighty wife;
sentences.n: χθιζός is an adjective ‘of yesterday’, doing the work of the adverb ‘yesterday’. ἐμυθεόμην is the imperfect of μυθέομαι ‘speak, tell’, uncontracted. τοι is taken here as the particle, nearly ‘you know’ (it could also be the dative ‘to you’, but σοί below already names the hearer). σοί ‘to you’ is the host in whose house Odysseus is speaking, and ἀλόχῳ ‘wife’ is his wife; ἰφθίμῃ is ‘mighty’, a general epithet of strength. The sentence explains why the tale breaks off.

sentences.t:
ἐχθρὸν δέ μοί ἐστιν
αὖτις ἀριζήλως εἰρημένα μυθολογεύειν.
sentences.tr:
echthron de moi estin
autis arizēlōs eirēmena mythologeuein.
sentences.l:
and hateful it is to me
again what has been very plainly said to tell over.”
sentences.i: and it is hateful to me to tell over again what has been told so plainly.”
sentences.n: ἐχθρόν is ‘hateful’; with ἐστιν and the infinitive it means ‘it is hateful to do’. μοί is ‘to me’. ἀριζήλως is the adverb ‘very plainly’ (ἀρι-, an intensive prefix, + δῆλος ‘clear’). εἰρημένα is the perfect passive participle of ἐρῶ ‘say’, neuter plural, ‘things said’. μυθολογεύειν is the verb of 450 in the infinitive, so that the question and its answer close on the same word. The tale Odysseus has been telling ends here. The closing quotation mark ends Odysseus’s whole tale, opened at 9.2 and reopened at 11.378.
